description: SelenoGrid is a solo entry by Hatim, built end to end: terrain pipeline, astronomy, ranking model, and interface. It is a static site with no backend. Everything runs in the browser, and the code, data, and methods are public on GitHub with a live GitHub Pages demo.
summary: SelenoGrid is a browser-based navigator for lunar south-pole landing sites. It puts 18 terrain points on one screen: the nine NASA Artemis candidate regions plus nine science and permanently shadowed reference sites. Choose a date and a window from 30 to 365 days, and it recomputes locally: sunlight share, direct-to-Earth visibility, longest continuous windows, time to the next sunset or earthset, slope, and horizon relief. Every site carries a 1,440-bin horizon ray-marched on the real 20 m LOLA elevation model, and Sun and Earth geometry is checked against JPL Horizons to about 0.02 degrees. A transparent weighted ranking, with visible weights and a Pareto frontier, shows which sites survive a given priority mix. A timeline heatmap, a 3D Moon, and any custom coordinate south of 80.15 S make the trade-off legible for planners, educators, and the public. No backend: the whole model runs in the browser from open NASA data.
details:
What it does. SelenoGrid compares lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in one workspace. A scenario bar sets the landing date, start hour, mission length (30, 90, 180, or 365 days), and sampling step. For every site it computes sunlight share of the window, direct-to-Earth visibility, longest unbroken Sun and Earth windows, the next sunset, sunrise, earthset and earthrise, local slope, and horizon relief. Terrain comes from a 1,440-bin horizon per site, ray-marched on the real LOLA 20 m elevation model out to 220 km with lunar curvature included. Sun and Earth positions come from a Meeus/IAU astronomy engine masked by that horizon, and they are validated against JPL Horizons to about 0.02 degrees. Events are bisection-refined to roughly one second, so the next sunset is not merely the nearest sample.

How it works. Everything is client-side. The app ships with a precomputed metrics set for the 18 curated points; changing the date, window, site selection, or weights recomputes live in the browser. The decision layer is a transparent TOPSIS ranking over four criteria (sunlight, Earth visibility, solar flux proxy, and slope as a cost), with exposed weights, presets, and a Pareto frontier that is independent of the weights. No learned model, no hidden coefficients. The Method view publishes the data contract, the visibility rule, the validation residuals, and the limits next to the formulas.

Benefits and impact. Mission planners get a fast screening layer: shortlist sites for a specific window and see which trade-offs dominate. Educators and the public get an intuitive explanation of why south-pole lighting and communication are hard, with plain-language summaries beside expert numbers. Because the method and provenance are visible, a result can be inspected and argued with rather than trusted blindly.

Tools and technology. React 19, TypeScript, and Vite; Tailwind CSS v4 with Radix primitives; Three.js for the Moon globe; Recharts plus custom SVG and canvas for horizons, heatmaps, and clearance charts; Lenis for smooth scrolling. Data preparation used Python and C tooling. Fonts are Inter, Space Grotesk, and Instrument Serif. The app is a static site on GitHub Pages with no backend and no API keys.

Creativity and considerations. The creative bet is that a landing site is a schedule, not a pin, so the whole interface is organised around time: event clocks, a scroll-scrubbed mission film, a daily heatmap, and time-to-sunset metrics. We deliberately kept the ranking explainable instead of optimising a single opaque score. We also decided what not to claim: representative points rather than official landing ellipses, screening accuracy rather than flight dynamics, no thermal or power sizing, no hazards below the 20 m terrain resolution, and custom pins clearly marked as a coarser 640 m screening grid.
